These are two very different worlds. Not saying there won't be hacks, but maybe not in the way we think.

Cell phones live and die by being cutting edge. Chip manufacturers are well known, drivers can be acquired and custom ROMs built. Sometimes a locked-down bootloader will slow the community for a bit, but in the end, they'll find an exploit.

With a car, the hardware is built and tailored for the vehicle. Cars are generally not swapped out as often as cell phones. As such, the drivers for the hardware and the hardware itself could be custom built for the vehicle and not well known. Take my Nissan Juke, for example. I have a rear-backing camera that displays on my dash when I back up. I thought, "Damn, I want to hack this so I can play movies on the screen!" Well, people have tried. The communication path between the camera, the computer and the display are all proprietary. No one knows quite how it works. There was a guy who busted out an oscilloscope and started probing contacts on microchips to try and reverse engineer it, but in the end, we don't have custom video on their display.

So, yes, I think people will find hack-ish things with such a vehicle. But by and large, if you think hacking a bootloader is hard, I bet this will be much more difficult. No KNOX tripping here. You fuck up, your car is now a giant paperweight. And a car is helluva lot more expensive than a phone.
